question: What person's name is associated with the fracture shown below? <image 1>

premises.text: A radiographic image of the forefoot displaying the five metatarsals and distal phalanges, revealing a transverse fracture at the proximal metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction of the fifth metatarsal with extensive surrounding callus formation.

An anteroposterior radiograph of a foot displays the five metatarsal bones and the phalanges of the toes, featuring a distinct transverse fracture at the proximal diaphysis of the fifth metatarsal (the lateral-most bone on the right side of the image), while the remaining metatarsals and phalanges appear structurally intact.

This is a grayscale radiograph of the forefoot showing the five metatarsals and the bases of the proximal phalanges, characterized by a large, expansile, lytic lesion with a multiloculated 'soap-bubble' appearance involving the proximal shaft and head of the first metatarsal, which also exhibits a transverse fracture line, while the second through fifth metatarsals and phalanges appear radiographically normal.

A grayscale radiograph of the forefoot displays a severe deformity of the first ray characterized by a large, bulbous exostosis at the medial base of the first metatarsal shaft, lateral deviation of the first metatarsal head, and medial deviation of the proximal phalanx of the hallux, with the remaining four metatarsals and phalanges visible to the left.

A grayscale X-ray radiograph of a human foot displaying the forefoot anatomy, specifically the five metatarsals and distal phalanges, showing a distinct transverse fracture at the base of the fifth metatarsal on the lateral side (left) and a large, bulbous enlargement of the proximal phalanx of the first toe (hallux) on the medial side (right).

A radiographic image of the forefoot displays the five metatarsals and their associated phalanges, with a distinct fracture and dislocation involving the first metatarsal (located on the right side of the image), where the metatarsal head is displaced dorsally and laterally relative to the first cuneiform, and the base of the metatarsal shows signs of fracture at the tarsometatarsal joint, while the remaining metatarsals appear relatively aligned.

An X-ray image of a human foot showing the five metatarsals and phalanges, with a transverse fracture visible at the base of the fifth metatarsal (lateral side) and a markedly enlarged, bulbous head of the first metatarsal (medial side).
An X-ray image of a human foot showing the five metatarsals and phalanges, with a distinct transverse fracture visible at the base of the fifth metatarsal bone on the left side of the image.

An anteroposterior X-ray of a human foot displaying the phalanges at the top and the five metatarsal bones extending downwards, characterized by a distinct transverse fracture line located at the proximal diaphysis (base) of the fifth metatarsal, which is the most lateral bone situated on the right side of the image.

A radiograph of the human forefoot showing the five metatarsals and proximal phalanges, with a distinct transverse fracture visible at the proximal diaphysis/metaphyseal junction of the lateral-most metatarsal (the fifth metatarsal).

An X-ray of the foot shows the five metatarsals and proximal phalanges, with a transverse fracture at the proximal diaphysis of the fifth metatarsal and a transverse fracture at the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe.

The image is a dorsal-plantar radiograph of a human foot displaying the five metatarsals and phalanges, where the first metatarsal (on the right) exhibits a prominent medial exostosis (bunion) and a severely fragmented, irregular head with a visible transverse fracture line separating it from the neck, while the proximal phalanx of the hallux is dislocated dorsally relative to the metatarsal head, contrasting with the relatively normal alignment and density of the other metatarsals.

The image displays a grayscale radiograph of a human forefoot showing the five metatarsal bones and their associated phalanges, with the first metatarsal (associated with the big toe having two phalanges) positioned on the left and the fifth metatarsal (associated with the little toe having three phalanges) positioned on the right, featuring a distinct transverse fracture line in the proximal diaphysis and significant bulbous bony enlargement at the proximal metaphysis of the fifth metatarsal.

An anteroposterior radiograph of the left foot reveals a transverse avulsion fracture at the base of the fifth metatarsal, showing a distinct bony fragment at the tuberosity, with the remaining metatarsals and phalanges appearing structurally intact.

The image is a grayscale radiograph of a human foot displaying the five metatarsal bones and the proximal phalanges of the toes, with a distinct fracture visible at the base of the first metatarsal located on the right side of the image.

A grayscale radiograph of the forefoot displaying the five metatarsals and phalanges, showing a distinct fracture line through the proximal phalanx of the first digit (great toe) located on the right side of the image.

This grayscale radiograph displays the forefoot and toes, revealing a displaced fracture of the proximal phalanx of the hallux (big toe) where the distal segment is angulated dorsally relative to the proximal segment, while the second through fifth toes and their corresponding metatarsals appear intact, with faint 'Kodak' text visible in the bottom left corner and partial numerical characters in the top left.

The image displays a black-and-white radiograph (X-ray) of a human foot, viewed from the dorsoplantar aspect with the toes oriented towards the top; the first metatarsal is located on the far right (medial side), appearing short and stout with a sesamoid bone underneath, while the fifth metatarsal is on the far left (lateral side), appearing longer and thinner, and exhibits a distinct transverse fracture at its proximal base near the tuberosity.

The image displays a radiograph of the forefoot and midfoot region, showing the five metatarsal bones arranged laterally to medially from left to right, with the corresponding distal phalanges visible proximally, featuring a distinct transverse fracture line located at the proximal diaphysis of the fifth metatarsal (the lateralmost metatarsal).

The image displays a radiograph of a hand featuring the five metacarpals and proximal phalanges, with a distinct intra-articular fracture at the base of the first metacarpal where a small proximal bone fragment remains articulating in the carpometacarpal joint while the shaft of the metacarpal is displaced and shows signs of sclerosis.

The image displays an anterior-posterior radiograph of a left foot, highlighting a transverse fracture in the proximal diaphysis of the fifth metatarsal (the lateralmost metatarsal on the far left), while the first metatarsal (medial, associated with the big toe on the right) and the second through fourth metatarsals appear intact and well-aligned with their respective phalanges.

A grayscale dorsoplantar radiograph of a foot displaying the skeletal anatomy, including the distal phalanges of the toes, the five metatarsal bones, and the proximal tarsal bones. The first metatarsal, which is the thickest bone located on the right side of the image, exhibits a fracture through the proximal diaphysis (shaft) characterized by a break in the cortical bone and displacement of the distal fragment relative to the proximal fragment. The adjacent second, third, fourth, and fifth metatarsals appear intact and aligned. The metatarsophalangeal joints are visible where the metatarsals articulate with the phalanges, and the soft tissue outlines surround the skeletal structures.

An X-ray image of a foot displays the five metatarsals and proximal phalanges, showing a transverse fracture located at the proximal diaphysis (shaft) of the fifth metatarsal (the lateral-most metatarsal on the left side of the image).

The image is a radiograph of the forefoot showing the five metatarsals; the fifth metatarsal (far left) exhibits a fracture at the proximal diaphysis (base) with associated sclerosis and callus formation, while the first metatarsal (far right) displays a large, bulbous, sclerotic mass at its proximal aspect, and the intermediate metatarsals appear relatively normal.

An anteroposterior radiograph of the foot reveals a complex injury involving the tarsometatarsal joint complex, characterized by a transverse fracture through the base of the second metatarsal, a fracture of the base of the fifth metatarsal, and a widened, disrupted first metatarsal base, with the metatarsal shafts and phalanges also visible.

An X-ray image displays the skeletal anatomy of a human foot, showing the five metatarsals and adjacent phalanges, with a distinct transverse fracture located in the proximal diaphysis of the fifth metatarsal (the lateral-most bone on the left side of the image).

The image is an anterior-posterior X-ray of a foot showing the phalanges and metatarsals, with a large, bulbous, sclerotic osteophyte at the base of the first metatarsal on the right, and a fracture of the proximal diaphysis of the fifth metatarsal on the left.

The image is a radiograph of a foot showing the five metatarsals and phalanges, where the first metatarsal (right side) exhibits a massive, irregular bony enlargement or exostosis at the head and neck, and the fifth metatarsal (far left) displays a transverse fracture at its proximal base/styloid process.

This is a grayscale radiograph of the forefoot displaying five metatarsals and the proximal-to-distal phalanges arranged vertically, with a distinct transverse fracture line visible in the proximal shaft of the fifth metatarsal (the bone located on the far left of the image), while the first metatarsal (on the far right) and the other intervening metatarsals appear intact, and there is no text or numerical label visible on the image.
A dorsoplantar radiograph of a right foot displaying the five metatarsals and phalanges, revealing a transverse fracture line across the proximal diaphysis of the fifth metatarsal bone.

The image displays an anteroposterior radiograph of a human foot showing the metatarsals and phalanges, with a distinct fracture visible at the base of the fifth metatarsal (the lateral-most metatarsal bone), characterized by a break in the continuity of the bone near the joint with the cuboid, while the other metatarsals appear relatively aligned and intact.

This image displays a dorsal-ventral radiograph of a left foot, visualizing the five metatarsal shafts and the phalanges of the five toes, where the first metatarsophalangeal joint exhibits a pathological fracture and dislocation characterized by the lateral and dorsal subluxation of the proximal phalanx of the hallux (big toe) relative to the metatarsal head, with associated displacement of the sesamoids, while the remaining four digits appear relatively aligned.

An anteroposterior radiograph of a foot displaying the phalanges of the five toes, characterized by a distinct transverse fracture at the base of the proximal phalanx of the hallux (great toe) with displacement and angulation of the proximal fragment.

An X-ray of a foot displays the phalanges of the five toes at the top and the five metatarsals in the midfoot, where the first metatarsal (on the right side of the image) is laterally and dorsally displaced relative to the tarsal bones, creating a widened space between the bases of the first and second metatarsals, and the proximal phalanx of the first toe is deviated medially, while the remaining metatarsals and distal phalanges appear relatively aligned.
